pages.title: Teacher Resources Overview
pages.html:
TEACHER-FACING · DO NOT SHARE WITH STUDENTS
Teacher Resources

This module is unpublished and visible only to teachers. It collects everything you need to run College Counseling & Critical Thinking. Keep it unpublished so students never see it.

What's here

  • Teacher Manual (PDF) — the full facilitator reference: how the course works, the intro/outro wrappers, AI & VR guidance, gradebook setup (55/25/15/5 weighting), rubrics for every graded item, weekly announcement scripts, a workload map, an adaptation guide for live 4-day-a-week sections, and the complete standards-coverage crosswalk.
  • Editable Syllabus (Word .docx) — a teacher-editable syllabus with bracketed fields for your name, office hours, and dates. Customize it in Word, then post or share it however your program prefers. A student-facing version is also live on the course Syllabus page.

Semester scope

This Canvas course is Semester 1 (Modules 1-3, the course's Quarter 1). Modules 4-6 (Money, Applying, College Essay, including the five-step Resume project) are built and will deploy as Semester 2.

Two deploy-time items flagged in the manual: before each cycle, verify the current Common App essay word limit (Module 6) and the current Bright Futures CLT concordance / Common App prompts (Module 5), since those change yearly.

Lesson 1.03
Focus
Your Personal Stock Inventory
Foundation for your resume and essay
Points
Assignment
25 pts
Lesson 1.03
Personal Stock Inventory
Assignment · 25 pts
📖 WHAT THIS ASSIGNMENT IS
An honest inventory of who you are right now
Built from your work in Lesson 1.03
You will create one Word document that captures your goals, your honest readiness, and the things you have done and care about. This is not busywork. It is the single document you will draw on when you build your resume and write your college essay later in the course, so the effort you put in now saves you effort twice over.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
If someone asked you today, "Who are you and where are you headed?" what is the honest, specific answer?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
In Word (through your Optima Microsoft 365 account), create a new document. Save it to your OneDrive and name it LastName_PersonalStockInventory.
2
Section 1 · Goals and interests. In 4 to 6 sentences, describe what you want your life and work to look like, and whether that points toward college. Be specific and honest rather than impressive.
3
Section 2 · Honest readiness. Rate yourself on study habits, time management, and working independently. For each, add one sentence explaining the rating. Use the self-placement you did in Lesson 1.03.
4
Section 3 · Accomplishments and interests. List at least 8 things you have done or are good at: jobs, chores you stuck with, activities, teams, responsibilities at home, skills you taught yourself, moments you are proud of. Then list 3 things you wish you could add to this list this year.
5
Section 4 · Reflection. In one paragraph, explain what this inventory shows you about your likely next step.
⚠️ DO THIS ONE YOURSELF
Write this from memory and honesty. An AI tool cannot recall your life or know what mattered to you, and a generic inventory will make your later resume and essay generic too. This is the step that makes everything after it sound like you.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All four sections are present and complete.
☐
The accomplishments list has at least 8 items, plus 3 things you want to add this year.
☐
Your writing is specific and honest, in your own voice.
☐
The reflection connects your accomplishments and interests to a possible next step.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1) Pts
Understanding of self
7 pts		 Goals and readiness are specific, honest, and clearly reasoned. Mostly specific and honest. General or partly guessed. Vague or missing. 7 pts
Quality of reasoning
6 pts		 Connects accomplishments and interests to a possible next step. Some connection made. Lists without connecting. Little reasoning. 6 pts
Completeness
6 pts		 All four sections complete; lists meet the minimums. Minor gaps. Several gaps. Largely incomplete. 6 pts
Clarity & honesty
6 pts		 Clear, own-voice writing that names real limits and hopes. Clear, mostly own voice. Some clarity issues. Unclear or generic. 6 pts
Total: 25 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Personal Stock Inventory
Upload your Word document (.docx) from OneDrive. Keep this file. You will reuse it in Modules 5 and 6.
Due: by the end of Module 1.
Be honest rather than impressive. Your teacher will read this and respond, and an honest inventory is far more useful to you than a polished one.

An Education Experience Company

Quarter / Module
Q1 · Module 2
Majors & Careers
Lesson
Lesson 2.03
Focus
Career & Major Exploration
Two careers, researched and weighed
Points
Assignment
25 pts
Lesson 2.03
Career & Major Exploration
Assignment · 25 pts
📖 WHAT THIS ASSIGNMENT IS
A real investigation of two careers you shortlisted
Built from your work in Lessons 2.01 through 2.03
You will research two careers that fit the patterns you found in your Personal Stock Inventory: what each career involves, the majors and education that lead to it, and what the data says about its pay and future. Then you will weigh the two against your own interests, strengths, and values. This is the thinking that turns "maybe I'll do something with..." into a direction you can act on.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Of the careers that fit who you are, what would each one actually require of you, and which requirement are you most willing to meet?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
In Word (through your Optima Microsoft 365 account), create a new document. Save it to your OneDrive and name it LastName_CareerMajorExploration.
2
Section 1 · Your two careers and why. Name the two careers you chose. In 3 to 4 sentences, explain how each one connects to your interests, strengths, or values, citing at least one specific item from your Personal Stock Inventory.
3
Section 2 · Career profiles. For each career, using the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook (bls.gov/ooh) and O*NET (onetonline.org), record: what the work involves day to day; the education typically required (degree level and common majors); median pay; and projected job growth. Note where each fact came from.
4
Section 3 · The education path. For each career, describe the path from where you are now: the major or majors that lead there, how many years of education, and any degrees beyond a bachelor's the career requires. If a career accepts many majors, say which one you would pick and why.
5
Section 4 · Reflection on fit. In one solid paragraph, weigh the two careers against each other using the three lenses (interests, strengths, values). Which fits you better right now, and why? What would you need to learn, build, or experience to be more sure? It is fine to conclude "neither, yet," as long as you show your reasoning.
⚠️ GET YOUR FACTS FROM THE SOURCE
An AI tool can suggest careers to consider or explain an unfamiliar job title, but its pay and growth figures may be outdated or invented. Pull your numbers directly from the BLS and O*NET pages, and write the reflection yourself: no tool knows which of your accomplishments mattered to you, and the fit judgment in Section 4 is the whole point of the assignment.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All four sections are present, and both careers are fully profiled.
☐
Education, pay, and growth facts come from BLS or O*NET, with the source noted.
☐
Each career is connected to specific evidence from your Personal Stock Inventory.
☐
The reflection weighs the two careers honestly through interests, strengths, and values, in your own voice.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1) Pts
Understanding of self
7 pts		 Career choices are clearly grounded in specific inventory evidence and the three lenses. Mostly grounded in real evidence about the student. Connections to self are general or asserted. Careers appear chosen at random. 7 pts
Quality of reasoning
6 pts		 Reflection weighs both careers with real trade-offs and reaches a reasoned judgment. Some genuine comparison made. Describes without comparing. Little reasoning shown. 6 pts
Completeness
6 pts		 All four sections complete; both profiles include education, pay, and growth with sources. Minor gaps. Several gaps or unsourced facts. Largely incomplete. 6 pts
Clarity & honesty
6 pts		 Clear, own-voice writing that names real doubts and open questions. Clear, mostly own voice. Some clarity issues. Unclear or generic. 6 pts
Total: 25 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Career & Major Exploration
Upload your Word document (.docx) from OneDrive. Keep this file. The careers and reasoning here feed directly into your college research in Module 3 and your resume and essay later on.
Due: by the end of Module 2.
You are not committing to either career by writing this. You are practicing the skill that matters: choosing a direction with evidence and being able to explain why.

assignments.title: College Shortlist
assignments.html:
Optima Academy Online
An Education Experience Company
COLLEGE COUNSELING & CRITICAL THINKING
Quarter / Module
Q1 · Module 3
Choosing Colleges
Lesson
Lesson 3.03
Focus
Your College Shortlist
The working list for Modules 4, 5, and 6
Points
Assignment
25 pts
Lesson 3.03
College Shortlist
Assignment · 25 pts
📖 WHAT THIS ASSIGNMENT IS
A researched comparison of real colleges against your own criteria
Built from your work in Lessons 3.01, 3.02, and 3.03
You will create one Word document that defines what fit means for you, then tests 3 to 5 real colleges against it with evidence you gathered yourself. This is not busywork. It becomes the working list you will price out in Module 4, track application deadlines for in Module 5, and draw on for your essay in Module 6, so research it as if you will use it. You will.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
If you had to defend each school on your list with evidence instead of its name, which schools would survive?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
In Word (through your Optima Microsoft 365 account), create a new document. Save it to your OneDrive and name it LastName_CollegeShortlist.
2
Section 1 · My fit criteria. List at least 5 criteria that define fit for you (for example: strength in your target program, size, distance from home, setting, campus culture, support services, cost range). Add one sentence per criterion explaining why it matters to you. At least 3 must be genuine fit factors from Lesson 3.03, not prestige signals.
3
Section 2 · The comparison table. Build a table in Word: one row per college (3 to 5 real colleges), one column per criterion. Fill every cell with a researched fact, not a guess. Include each school's type (public or private, two-year or four-year, approximate size) and its first-year retention rate.
4
Section 3 · School notes. For each college, write three short lines: one strength that genuinely excites you, one concern or open question, and where your evidence came from (the program's own pages, College Scorecard, a visit or virtual tour, a college guide, or a pattern across student reviews).
5
Section 4 · Reflection. In one paragraph, name the school that currently leads your list and defend it using your fit criteria. If no school leads yet, that is a legitimate answer: say what additional evidence would settle it.
⚠️ WHERE AI HELPS, AND WHERE IT DOES NOT
An AI tool can suggest candidate schools and help you organize a table. It cannot know your fit criteria, and it sometimes states outdated program details, sizes, or rates with confidence. Every fact in your table must be verified by you against the college's own site or College Scorecard, and the criteria and reflection must be your own thinking. Your teacher is reading for your judgment, not a tool's summary.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All four sections are present and complete, with 3 to 5 real colleges in the table.
☐
At least 5 fit criteria, each with a reason, and at least 3 that are genuine fit factors.
☐
Every table cell holds a researched fact, including each school's type and first-year retention rate, and Section 3 names your sources.
☐
The reflection defends a front-runner (or names the missing evidence) using fit factors, not prestige.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1) Pts
Understanding of fit
7 pts		 Criteria are personal, specific, and genuinely fit-based. Mostly personal and specific. Generic or partly prestige-driven. Vague or missing. 7 pts
Quality of reasoning
6 pts		 Comparisons rest on researched evidence with sources noted; the reflection follows from the table. Mostly evidence-based; some reasoning gaps. Assertions with little evidence. Little reasoning or research shown. 6 pts
Completeness
6 pts		 All four sections complete; 3 to 5 colleges fully compared, retention rates included. Minor gaps. Several gaps. Largely incomplete. 6 pts
Clarity & honesty
6 pts		 Clear, own-voice writing that names real concerns as well as attractions. Clear, mostly own voice. Some clarity issues. Unclear or generic. 6 pts
Total: 25 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: College Shortlist
Upload your Word document (.docx) from OneDrive. Keep this file. You will reuse it in Modules 4, 5, and 6.
Due: by the end of Module 3.
A shortlist full of honest evidence and open questions is far more useful than one full of famous names. Your teacher will read this and respond with feedback you can build on all semester.

discussions.title: College Myths Discussion
discussions.html:
Name one belief about college that you (or people you know) once held that turned out to be a myth. State the reality, and explain the reasoning or evidence that changed your mind. Keep it to about 4-6 sentences.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, add one point that strengthens it. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

CriterionFull (2)Partial (1)Missing (0)
Names a myth and its realityClear myth + accurate realityVague or only one of the twoAbsent
ReasoningExplains what changed the student's mind with a real reason or exampleAsserts without supportAbsent
Reply to a classmateSubstantive: strengthens or respectfully challenges reasoningThin ("I agree!")Absent

discussions.title: Career-First or Major-First Discussion
discussions.html:
You have now learned both approaches: career-first (pick the destination, work backward to the education) and major-first (pick a field you love, work forward to the doors it opens). Which approach fits you better right now, and why? Name the approach, then defend your choice with at least one specific piece of evidence about yourself: an interest, a strength, a value, or something from your Personal Stock Inventory. Keep it to about 4-6 sentences.

Then reply to one classmate who chose the other approach. Identify one strength of their reasoning, or respectfully point out something they may not have considered.

CriterionFull (2)Partial (1)Missing (0)
Names an approach and a clear positionClear choice with an accurate description of the approachVague choice or muddled descriptionAbsent
ReasoningDefends the choice with specific personal evidenceAsserts without supportAbsent
Reply to a classmateSubstantive: engages the other approach's reasoningThin ("I agree!")Absent

discussions.title: Fit over Prestige Discussion
discussions.html:
Name the two fit factors that matter most to you in a college (for example: location and setting, campus culture, size and class style, support services, distance from home, or cost). For each one, explain the reasoning: what about your goals, habits, or life makes this factor matter? Then apply the lesson's test: would each factor still matter if no one else ever heard where you went? Keep it to about 4-6 sentences.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree that their factors are fit factors rather than prestige signals? If so, add one point that strengthens their reasoning. If not, respectfully explain where you think a prestige signal snuck in.

CriterionFull (2)Partial (1)Missing (0)
Names two fit factorsTwo genuine fit factors, clearly statedOne factor, or factors that are really prestige signalsAbsent

syllabus_html:
College Counseling & Critical Thinking
Semester 1 Syllabus · Modules 1-3

Course Overview

College Counseling & Critical Thinking is a half-credit, one-semester elective for students planning their path after high school. The course runs asynchronously in Canvas at roughly 250 minutes of work per week; some sections also meet live four days a week using this same content.

The course has two internal quarters. Quarter 1 (Modules 1-3) covers understanding higher education, choosing a career or major, and building a college shortlist. Quarter 2 (Modules 4-6), covering paying for college, applying, and the college essay, is published separately.

Modules This Semester

ModuleFocusMajor Project
1. IntroductionPlanning your path; how memory and study workPersonal Stock Inventory
2. Majors & CareersCareer-first vs. major-first decision makingCareer & Major Exploration
3. CollegesFit over prestige; types of collegesCollege Shortlist

How Your Grade Is Weighted

CategoryWeightWhat it includes
Practice & Comprehension55%Auto-graded quizzes after each lesson
Discussions & Reflections25%One discussion per module (post + reply)
Major Projects15%One teacher-reviewed project per module
Wrappers & Participation5%Opening check-ins and wrap-up reflections (completion credit)

Late & Missing Work

There is no per-day late penalty. Unsubmitted work remaining at the end of the semester scores zero. Work submitted in the final 14 days of the semester receives a 10% deduction.

Getting Help

Message your teacher through Canvas, email, or attend office hours. In an on-demand course, the best move is to ask early rather than waiting until the night before something is due.
